supported.clue: The Constitution divides the government into three branches: legislative (Congress), executive (President), and judicial (courts). No one branch has all the power.

on_grade.clue: This constitutional principle divides governmental authority among three distinct branches — legislative, executive, and judicial — to prevent any single person or group from accumulating too much power.

advanced.clue: Madison drew directly on Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws in designing this structural principle, though he modified the French philosopher's model by giving each branch partial control over the others rather than keeping them fully independent.

supported.clue: Each branch of government has the power to limit the other two. Congress can override a presidential veto. The President can veto laws. Courts can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

on_grade.clue: This system ensures that no branch of government can act without some form of oversight from the others — through mechanisms like the presidential veto, congressional override, Senate confirmation, and judicial review.

advanced.clue: Madison argued in Federalist No. 51 that this system works not because leaders are virtuous, but because 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' — structuring government so that self-interest itself prevents tyranny.

supported.clue: In this 1803 Supreme Court case, Chief Justice John Marshall declared that the Supreme Court has the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution. This power is now used regularly by the Court.

on_grade.clue: Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), this principle — not explicitly written in the Constitution — gives the Supreme Court the authority to declare acts of Congress or the President unconstitutional.

advanced.clue: Marshall's opinion in Marbury was a masterpiece of political maneuvering — he ruled against his own Federalist ally to avoid a confrontation Jefferson could win, while establishing the far more consequential power that would define the Court's role for two centuries.

supported.clue: In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a state could not tax a federal bank — establishing that when federal and state laws conflict, the federal law wins.

on_grade.clue: This 1819 Supreme Court ruling established two critical precedents: that Congress has implied powers beyond those explicitly listed, and that federal law is supreme over conflicting state law.

advanced.clue: Marshall's opinion introduced the doctrine of implied powers by interpreting the Necessary and Proper Clause expansively — ruling that 'necessary' meant 'useful,' not 'indispensable,' a reading that dramatically broadened congressional authority.

supported.clue: Changing the Constitution is difficult on purpose. A change must be proposed by two-thirds of Congress (or a convention), then approved by three-fourths of the states.

on_grade.clue: The framers made this process deliberately difficult — requiring supermajority approval at both the proposal and ratification stages — to prevent temporary majorities from easily altering the nation's fundamental law.

advanced.clue: The difficulty of this process has had a paradoxical effect: it has pushed constitutional change into the courts, with the Supreme Court reinterpreting existing text rather than new amendments supplying most of the Constitution's evolution over two centuries.

advanced.clue: The equal Senate representation secured by small states in this compromise has had enduring consequences — giving Wyoming the same two votes as California, a structural counter-majoritarian feature that the framers accepted to achieve ratification.

advanced.clue: This provision gave the slaveholding South a substantial bonus in House seats and Electoral College votes — historians estimate it gave Virginia alone about a dozen extra representatives, contributing directly to the domination of the early presidency by southern slaveholders.

supported.clue: The Constitution divides power between the national government and state governments. Each level has its own powers, and some powers are shared.

on_grade.clue: This system divides governmental authority between a national government and the states — with some powers exclusive to each level, some concurrent, and the Tenth Amendment reserving to states all powers not delegated to the federal government.

advanced.clue: The Constitution created a federal system that was genuinely novel — neither a confederation of sovereign states nor a unitary national government, but a compound republic in which both levels governed individuals directly rather than through each other.

advanced.clue: The framers debated whether to give the executive an absolute veto — as the British Crown possessed — or a qualified one subject to legislative override; the compromise qualified veto reflected their fear of both executive tyranny and legislative excess.

advanced.clue: The First Amendment's two religion clauses — Establishment and Free Exercise — have generated persistent constitutional tension: the government may neither promote religion nor burden its practice, a balance the Court has struggled to define consistently across two centuries.
